awd_titl_txt: IIBR RoL:  Collaborative Research:  A Rules Of Life Engine (RoLE) Model to Uncover Fundamental Processes Governing Biodiversity
awd_abstract_narration:
An unprecedented opportunity to advance understanding of the biological rules that govern the diversity and dynamics of life now exists thanks to the large quantity and variety of data that are becoming increasingly available.  This goal of understanding biodiversity dynamics is enabled at a critical moment when human systems are disrupting those very dynamics. However, the scientific and computational tools needed to derive understanding from data are still missing.  Such tools need to be accessible to a broad community of users, thereby catalyzing involvement and innovation.  This project will (1) build a computational model for multiple aspects of biodiversity-species abundance, genetic, functional, and phylogenetic; (2) use and refine this model by testing major hypotheses about the generation and maintenance of biodiversity in three exemplar systems; (3) make the model accessible to the scientific community by building an open-source platform to prepare diverse data sources and run the model; and (4) create pedagogically effective courses and workshops to enable students, researchers, and stakeholders from many backgrounds to understand biodiversity theory and the data science tools needed to test those theories with data.

The Rules of Life Engine (RoLE) model will be a mechanistic, simulation-based hypothesis-testing and data synthesis framework enabling scientists with multi-dimensional biodiversity data to generate and test hypotheses about the processes driving biodiversity patterns. The RoLE model will apply new techniques in machine learning to fit models to high dimensional, cross-scale data. The model will simulate eco-evolutionary community assembly building from individual-based ecological and genetic neutral models with added non-neutral, trait-based competition and environmental filtering. New species and traits will arise through long time scale evolution in the meta-community and rapid evolution in the local community. Population genetics and species abundances in the local community will be modeled through birth, death, immigration, and mutation. The project research team will refine and illustrate the use of the RoLE model by testing four hypothesized rules of life across three bio-geographic systems for which multi-scale biodiversity data are now available. The hypotheses address the relative roles of immigration versus speciation in community assembly, how species interactions influence diversity, how different assembly histories determine the strength of species interactions, and whether/how systems come to equilibrium. The project leaders have established a network of 14 collaborators, including the National Ecological Observatory Network, who will use the RoLE model in their diverse systems and propagate wider adoption. In order to further reduce barriers to use, the RoLE model framework will be made available as open source software, including an R language Shiny App interface with standardized metadata outputs to promote reproducibility and sharing. The insights gained from the RoLE model are of direct relevance to conservation, e.g., whether or not communities are assembled primarily by speciation or immigration strongly determines their response to anthropogenic pressures and optimal conservation management. To encourage participation in quantitative biodiversity research, the project leaders will develop a massively open online course through the Santa Fe Institute?s Complexity Explorer program using the RoLE model as an interactive teaching tool. In conjunction with Data Carpentry and Software Carpentry, the research team will also provide an in-person data science training workshop. Results from the RoLE project can be found at https://role-model.github.io.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Despite decades of research, understanding how biodiversity is generated and maintained remains an elusive challenge. Historically, two bottlenecks likely account for much of this challenge: insufficient theory and models of biodiversity and insufficient magnitude of data. Recent advances in ecological and evolutionary theory have produced insights about the roles of dispersal limitation, evolutionary history, and ecological interactions among populations. Recent advances in high throughput sequencing have revolutionized the scale at and quantity with which biodiversity data can be collected. The fact that these advances have not resolved debate about the processes underlying biodiversity points to another bottleneck: advances have been largely siloed without integrating insights and approaches. Our project aspires to build connections across theories, models, and high throughput biodiversity data. Specifically our aims are to 1) build a computational model for multiple aspects of biodiversity—species abundance, genetic, functional, and phylogenetic; 2) use and refine this model by testing major hypotheses about the generation and maintenance of biodiversity; 3) make the model available to the scientific community by building an open-source platform to prepare diverse data sources and run the model; and 4) create pedagogically effective courses and workshops to enable students, researchers, and stakeholders from many backgrounds to understand biodiversity theory and the data science tools needed to test those theories with data.

 

Intellectual Merit: We developed the Rules of Life Engine (RoLE) model to integrate multiple models of biodiversity and unify predictions across species abundance, genetic diversity, functional traits, and phylogenetic relationships. The model generates temporally explicit joint predictions spanning equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions, capturing information at ecological, microevolutionary, and macroevolutionary timescales. One insight from this work is that disparate models of biodiversity, those based on neutrality or ecological niches, those without regard for evolutionary history, and those integrally based on genetic relatedness, can be integrated into a single computational model using individual based simulations. Another insight is that the parameters of this complex model can be accurately fit to real data using simulation-based likelihood-free inference. This type of inference relies on machine learning techniques. Our study of these techniques showed that eco-evolutionary models are most reliably inferred when multiple data axes are jointly predicted, confirming the contribution of continuing to overcome the data and modeling bottlenecks in understanding biodiversity. 

 

Fitting the model to real data revealed how different ecological assemblages relate to each other based on similarities and differences in the processes underlying their dynamics and persistence. This is a unique contribution of our work: the ability to contextualize and compare assemblages not in terms of shared taxa, but in terms of shared or divergent processes. Our work with real data also identified areas for model refinement, especially how competitive interactions within and among species are modeled. These improvements were incorporated in the open source software implementing the RoLE model in the R programming language, roleR and roleshiny.

 

Broader Impacts: Understanding biodiversity comes at a time when stewarding it through rapid global change is of heightened importance. While our model cannot yet be used directly in conservation, it lays the foundation for being able to predict biodiversity change under different scenarios of global change and human intervention (e.g. restoration). The more researchers and conservation practitioners who can work with this and other models, as well as high throughput data streams, the more likely we will be as a community to see novel applications for societal good. Therefore one of our primary goals was creating education and training materials in biodiversity data science and computational ecology and evolution. We successfully incorporated the RoLE model as a teaching tool in a new graduate curriculum on eco-evolutionary theory and in an intensive three day workshop curriculum on biodiversity data science. We offered the graduate course and the intensive workshop to broad cross sections of students and early career professionals during the course of this award, in total reaching 30 participants in the workshop and 14 graduate students in the course.

 

In addition to students and early career researchers supported through our teaching and curriculum development, this award directly supported the career development and mentorship (through direct financial support, support of their advisor, or both) of 8 undergraduate students, 6 graduate students, 2 postdocs, and 1 early career professional.
